summary:
Iran is among the most restrictive environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty, and the UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes, and Human Rights Watch documented two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005, the enforcement backdrop against which any visitor is assessed.

Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional. A 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini permits gender-reassignment surgery, which may be state-subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder", and Article 20, Clause 14 allows a person who has had sex reassignment surgery to change name and gender on the birth certificate by court order, with corrected identity documents reportedly issued efficiently and transparently. The Home Office report sets the limits: recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; the surgery available is invasive and often sub-standard; and an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

Identity documents can themselves expose a holder. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that this disclosure identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination.

State pressure operates in public space as well as in paperwork. Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas, an official advisory restricting trans visibility, and the 2017 US State Department report noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons.

Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility in an open letter published by HRANA.

Raids on private gatherings produce mass arrests and threats of execution. An IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province on 13 April 2017 involved agents reportedly firing weapons and electric Tasers; those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led into the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008 police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men, held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity, and in January 2008 Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) were arrested in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges.

Judicial outcomes remain lethal. Two youths were reportedly hanged in north-eastern Iran in 2006 for "sex crimes"; in 2022 two gay men in Maragheh received death sentences for "sodomy by force", a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, later commuted to life in prison. The death penalty is legal from 18 for adults and from 15 for murder, and the 2017 US State Department report raised concerns about LGBTI minors. In May 2021 Ali Monfared, aged 20, was murdered allegedly by relatives.

6Rang documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct, part of the evidentiary practice attached to these prosecutions.

The medical regime is coercive as well as permissive. The state funds gender-reassignment surgery while placing pressure on Iranian trans people to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty; surgery is invasive and often sub-standard and is framed publicly as protection. Two 2024–2025 media investigations describe foreign patients travelling for the same subsidised procedures while local transitions are effectively forced.

There is no same-sex marriage or civil union recognition and no legislation addressing discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, leaving that role to exiled groups.

Displacement is systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on SOGI (February 2025), "They See Us as Criminals", surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran, 96% of them from ethnic minorities, documenting the persecution driving departure; a further 6Rang submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review at the 48th session (January–February 2025) catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
The asylum landscape for people leaving Iran is mixed and inconsistent, which bears on any trans visitor facing removal. The UNHCR rejected a 2001 request from an Iranian man who had entered a country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005 and Sweden rejected a similar appeal the same year. The Netherlands halted deportations of gay men to Iran temporarily in March 2006, when the Dutch Immigration Minister stated there was "no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay", then reversed under pressure and confirmed in October 2006 that Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who took their own lives when faced with removal, while campaign-backed cases including Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in grants. LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023.

Advocacy capacity inside the country is nil by design, so documentation of conditions comes from external bodies: 6Rang, Outright International, HRANA, Human Rights Watch and foreign government reporting each supply independent accounts that broadly agree on criminalisation and enforcement, and differ mainly in emphasis rather than finding.

Iran's conditional tolerance has an external dimension that distorts the picture for outsiders: trans medical tourism is reported to be growing, with foreign patients accessing state-subsidised surgery that local trans people receive only under pressure to conform to a binary transition and accept invasive, often sub-standard procedures.

Ethnicity compounds exposure. The 6Rang survey of 25 displaced LGBTIQ+ people found 96% came from ethnic minorities, indicating that persecution is not evenly distributed across the population.
localsOnly:
Residents who complete the surgical and legal process receive concrete state support. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery.

The legal route to corrected documents runs through Article 20, Clause 14, which permits a person who has had sex reassignment surgery to change name and gender on birth certification by court order, with corrected identity documents reportedly issued efficiently and transparently. Supporters of reassignment also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a "rational benefit", subject to approval by a doctor.

HIV and sexual-health services are generally accessible to residents: HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. The government approved a booklet explaining condoms for distribution to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood has noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programmes for LGBTQ people can be developed.

Political organising around these issues is impossible domestically. Because the government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, that role has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran.

Family authority governs marriage in practice as well as law: traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry, gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public, and Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages.
outOfScopeNotes:
Several document-level specifics rest on a single compiled reference rather than primary legislation in this inventory: the numbering of Article 20, Clause 14 and Article 215, the wording of the military identity card exemption subsection, and 6Rang's warning about that subsection are not corroborated by a statutory text here and remain unresolved.

The Home Office report's statement that recognition requires sterilisation is not tied to a named provision in the inventory; the legal basis and current enforceability of the sterilisation condition are unresolved.

The cash grant and loan figures date from the mid-2000s and are given in the conversion used by the source; whether those amounts remain in force, and at what real value after inflation, is not sourced.

The RFE/RL report of Tehran authorities warning transgender people away from busy areas carries no date in the inventory, so the currency of that advisory is unresolved.

The scale of trans medical tourism to Iran is asserted by two media reports without patient numbers or revenue figures in this inventory.

Whether courts currently grant Article 20 name and gender changes without surgery, and how quickly, is described only as "reportedly efficient" in secondary sourcing; no case-level verification is available here.
